name: The bark shed at Miller and Hall's tanyard

documented_range.note: NO SOURCE RECORD DATES THIS BUILDING, BECAUSE NO SOURCE RECORD NAMES IT. The bracket is the tanyard's own, carried across without being re-argued: `miller_tannery` - the log house Samuel Miller's brother John used as a tannery, with Benjamin Hall in from 1832 - carries 1831-01-01 to 1835-12-31, and a yard building that serves that tannery cannot honestly claim to have stood before it. Graded `reconstructed`, as the building is.

change_note: One phase. This is a reconstruction of a works building the plant's own record says is missing, not a record of a building anybody named, so it has no history to divide into phases and inventing one would be inventing twice.

placement.position_note:
INVENTED, AND SEATED BY THE WORKS RULE BELOW. THE TANYARD RUNS NORTH, BEHIND THE TANNERY, AND THAT IS WHERE THE GROUND IS. `miller_tannery` stands at bearing 180 with its face south toward Samuel Miller's house and tavern; behind it is north, on the point of land between the North Branch and the main stem. The two yard buildings stand side by side across that back yard, both with their front walls on one line 5.20 m north of the tannery's north wall - the cart yard figure T-1640 derived from `data/yard/town_trade_goods.json` - and each with one wall on one of the tannery's own two side walls, so the yard is framed by the three buildings rather than scattered behind one. THIS BUILDING takes the WEST end: its east wall stands on local E 7.000, which is the tannery's own west wall line, and its front wall stands at local N 83.200. MEASURED ON THIS SEAT, over a 25 x 25 lattice on the placed polygon: the ground stands 1.129 m to 1.130 m above the committed water surface - dry, and flat to a millimetre, with 0.001 m of relief across the whole rectangle; `intrusion` reads it clear of all 33 platted corridors; and the nearest committed footprint is the tannery's own north wall at 5.20 m. WORKING UNCERTAINTY: this is the best-placed of the four noxious trades - the tannery's own position is `inferred` on Andreas's 'just north of Miller's tavern' rather than reconstructed - so the SITE is about as good as this band gets and the BUILDING is still entirely invented.

THE WORKS RULE, STATED ONCE AND APPLIED SIX TIMES (T-1709). Every one of the four documented noxious trades on the branches records, in its own footprint note, that the works are outside its polygon: `newberry_dole_slaughterhouse_south_branch` says 'the pens, the yard and the barrelling and salting space that a packing operation needs are outside the footprint and outside this archetype, which builds a building rather than a works'; `miller_tannery` says 'a tannery is its yard - bark mill, lime pits, tan vats, drying sheds, and a water supply - and none of that is in this polygon or in the model'; `clybourn_slaughterhouse` says 'what is not modelled is arguably the bigger half'; `elston_soap_candle_manufactory` gives a shed 'big enough for a rendering kettle, a cooling and moulding floor and an ash leach' and nothing beside it. This building is one of the works those four sentences name, and NOTHING ATTESTS IT. It is placed by a rule and not by a plate. THE RULE: (1) a works building stands BEHIND its plant, on the side away from the water, because the plant's own bearing puts its working face on the water and the ground behind it is what is left; (2) the gap between the plant's wall and the works' wall is 5.20 m, the cart yard T-1640 derived from `data/yard/town_trade_goods.json` - 1.00 m of clearance from the wall a wagon stands at, plus the 3.20 m of ground a parked wagon needs, plus 1.00 m from the wall opposite - and the same 5.20 m separates one works building from the next, so the whole band is set out on one committed figure; (3) the works take the plant's own bearing, so the yard between them is square and the doors face it; (4) where the ground behind the plant is a platted street corridor, the works stand ALONG the bank instead, in the order the work runs, on a line that keeps them 0.50 m clear of that corridor's own edge - which is what the South Branch band does, because Market Street's corridor runs E 73.00 to E 97.00 at this reach and the plant itself stands 1.30 m inside it. THE FOUR PREDICATES each seat is held to, on a 25 x 25 lattice over the placed polygon: dry in the committed heightfield (`data/terrain/epochs/e1834_harbor_cut`, WATER_SURFACE_M = 0), relief inside the 0.30 m `generate_block_infill.MAX_RELIEF_M` allows, clear of all 33 platted corridors (`tools/plat_corridors.intrusion`), and clear of every footprint the committed tree already places. docs/RESEARCH/branch_noxious_works.md carries the readings and docs/LIBERTIES.md L283 owns the invention.
placement.symbolic_location: On the point of land at the forks, in the yard behind John Miller's tannery, at the west end of the back yard with its east wall on the tannery's own west wall line and its door facing south across the yard.

footprint.note: INVENTED. 2.4384 x 4.8768 m is 8 x 16 ft, inside family A4's band (6-8 ft front, 12-18 ft deep) - the crosswalk's woodshed and storage outbuilding. A bark shed is a store: hemlock or oak bark brought in, kept dry, and ground as it is wanted. The size is the family's and nothing states that this yard had a bark shed at all. Every number is invented.

construction.note: Notched logs, the archetype's `log`, because the building it serves is one - the sources call the tannery 'a log house ... that he used as a tannery' and this is the oldest of the four noxious sites, standing from 1831 on the point where the first log building in the settlement went up. At 2.44 m on its short side it clears the archetype's 2.2 m LOG_MIN_DIM_M, below which corner notching eats the wall. The fabric is reasoned from its neighbour and is not attested.

wall_height_m.note: About 7 ft 10 in, a shade over the archetype's size-aware default of 2.31 m for this plan. A man stands inside and forks bark; nothing here needs more. Invented.

roof_type.note: 4.88 m of depth is inside the 5.0 m at which `default_roof_type` gives a shed roof. Invented.

roof_pitch_deg.note: The archetype's default for a shed roof; the rise over this run is 1.59 m against a 2.4 m wall, inside SHED_RISE_RATIO_MAX. Invented.

door.note: 1.35 m clear - wide enough to barrow bark through, narrower than a wagon door, and it stands on a 2.44 m wall which carries it with a jamb either side. Invented.

door_side.note: The `front` elevation is the max-y wall, which at this bearing faces SOUTH, onto the yard between this shed and the tannery. Invented.

function.note: The closed vocabulary has no `bark shed`; `woodshed_or_storage_shed` is family A4's own name and a bark shed is a store. The specific use is in the record's NAME and in this note. The use comes from the tannery's own record, which says in as many words that 'a tannery is its yard - bark mill, lime pits, tan vats, drying sheds, and a water supply - and none of that is in this polygon or in the model'. This is the first of those. No occupant is claimed.

research_note: A RECONSTRUCTED YARD BUILDING AT THE SETTLEMENT'S FIRST FACTORY - T-1709, of T-1203. WHAT IS HELD: Andreas and DRLOIH for the tannery, its fabric, its year, its partner Benjamin Hall and its direction from Samuel Miller's tavern. WHAT IS INVENTED: this building and every attribute of it, including that it existed. WHAT IS STILL NOT MODELLED: the lime pits, the tan vats and the bark mill itself, which are pits and machinery rather than buildings - the tannery's record names them and this one does not discharge them. WHAT WOULD UPGRADE IT: any account of Miller and Hall's tanyard, or the Chicago Democrat's advertisements. Built under the owner's standing ruling of 2026-08-18.
